title: Into Egypt, Taking Jeremiah with Them
summary: Azariah, Johanan, and the other leaders call Jeremiah a liar and blame Baruch for turning him against them. They take the whole remnant, including Jeremiah and Baruch, to Egypt and settle at Tahpanhes. There God has Jeremiah bury large stones at the entrance to Pharaoh's building and announces that Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne on that very spot and burn the temples of Egypt's gods.
story: Chapter 42 ended with the remnant's promise to obey and Jeremiah's warning that they would not. This chapter shows how quickly the promise broke. The leaders don't argue with God's word; they deny that it is God's word at all. Then the people who had been left in the land by Babylon, and those who had come home from neighboring countries, leave it, reversing the brief regathering of 40:11-12. In a bitter irony, the exodus runs backward: the descendants of those God brought out of Egypt now walk back into it. Jeremiah goes with them, apparently against his will, and even in Egypt the word of God follows. The chapter sets the scene for Jeremiah's last recorded message in chapter 44.
historical:
Tahpanhes (verse 7) was a frontier town on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta, known to Greek writers as Daphnae and identified with the site of Tell Defenneh. It lay on the main route from Canaan into Egypt, and in this period it housed a garrison that included foreign soldiers, among them Greeks serving Egypt's pharaohs. When Flinders Petrie excavated there in 1886, he found a large fortified building with a brick platform in front of it and suggested it was the place described in verse 9. The local name for the ruin, which Petrie reported as meaning the castle of the Jew's daughter, has been connected by some with the king's daughters of verse 6, but that is a later local tradition and not evidence. The Pharaoh at this time was Hophra (Apries), who reigned about 589 to 570 BC (44:30).

Did Nebuchadnezzar invade Egypt as verses 10 to 13 announce? A damaged Babylonian tablet in the British Museum refers to a campaign against Egypt in Nebuchadnezzar's thirty-seventh year, about 568/567 BC, in the reign of Pharaoh Amasis. The text is broken and doesn't say how far the Babylonians went. There is no evidence that Babylon conquered or occupied Egypt, and scholars differ on how to read the prophecy's fulfillment (see the hard question below).
cultural:
Burying stones in the brick pavement at a building's entrance (verse 9) was a sign-act, a symbolic action performed in public to make a prophecy visible, much like Jeremiah's linen belt (chapter 13) or his yoke (chapter 27). The stones mark the spot where a foreign king will one day set his throne, a picture of conquest. A royal pavilion or canopy was spread over a conqueror's throne when he sat to judge the defeated, as Babylonian kings did in the field (39:3-5).

The temple of the sun (verse 13) translates Beth-shemesh, the house of the sun, probably the Hebrew name for the great Egyptian city of On, called Heliopolis by the Greeks, just northeast of modern Cairo. Heliopolis was the center of the worship of the sun god Ra, and its temples were famous for their stone obelisks, the sacred pillars of this verse. Taking a defeated nation's gods captive meant carrying off the statues from their temples, a common practice of Assyrian and Babylonian conquerors that proclaimed the superiority of their own gods.
literary: The chapter has two parts: the narrative of refusal and departure (verses 1 to 7), and a sign-act with its explanation (verses 8 to 13). The narrator repeats the key charge twice: the people did not obey the voice of the LORD (verses 4 and 7). Their accusation in verse 2, “You are lying”, uses the word sheqer, which Jeremiah had used throughout the book of false prophets and false trust; now it is turned against him. The phrase “My servant Nebuchadnezzar” (verse 10) repeats a startling title from 25:9 and 27:6, making clear that the Babylonian king acts under God's direction. The image of Nebuchadnezzar wrapping himself in Egypt “as a shepherd wraps himself in his garment” (verse 12) pictures how easily he will take the land, like a shepherd pulling on a cloak.

outline.t: The leaders accuse Jeremiah of lying
The remnant goes down to Egypt, taking Jeremiah and Baruch
A sign-act: stones buried at Pharaoh's building
Nebuchadnezzar will come and burn Egypt's temples

doctrines.note: God calls Nebuchadnezzar “My servant” and says he himself will send for him (verse 10). The empires of the world, even pagan ones, serve God's purposes, whether they know it or not.
The gods of Egypt, whose temples and pillars seemed permanent, will be burned and carried off. The people fled to Egypt for safety, but Egypt's gods cannot even save themselves.
The leaders are called arrogant (verse 2). Their refusal is rooted in pride, which will not accept a word that contradicts its own plan and so declares the messenger a liar.

words.note: Sheqer, a lie, falsehood, or deception. It is one of Jeremiah's signature words: he condemned trust in lying words (7:4) and prophets who prophesied lies (14:14, 23:25). Here the leaders throw the word back at him. The irony is that they are the ones believing a lie about the safety of Egypt.

Zed, arrogant, presumptuous. It describes people who act in proud defiance, especially against God. The Psalms often set the arrogant against those who fear God (Psalm 119:21). The narrator uses it to name what drove the leaders' decision.

Eved, servant or slave. When God calls Nebuchadnezzar “My servant” (verse 10), it doesn't mean the king worshiped Israel's God, but that God used him as an agent to carry out his purposes, as a master uses a servant.

Matstsevah, a standing stone or sacred pillar. Israel's neighbors set up such pillars in their worship, and the law ordered Israel to tear down those of the Canaanites (Deuteronomy 12:3). Here the word likely refers to the obelisks of Heliopolis.

christ: The remnant's return to Egypt reverses the exodus, the great act of redemption in which God brought his people out of slavery. The Gospel of Matthew records that the infant Jesus was taken to Egypt to escape Herod and then brought back, and Matthew applies to him the words of Hosea 11:1, God calling his son out of Egypt (Matthew 2:15). Where the remnant in this chapter went down to Egypt in disobedience and fear, Jesus goes down and comes up in obedience, retracing Israel's story and fulfilling it. That is a pattern the New Testament itself draws, although it doesn't draw it from this chapter directly. The chapter also shows the prophet going where his people go, even into their disobedience, a picture of faithful presence that finds its fullest form in Christ's sharing our life.

hard.q: Did Nebuchadnezzar actually conquer Egypt as Jeremiah predicted?
hard.a: The historical record is limited. A fragmentary Babylonian tablet mentions a campaign against Egypt around 568/567 BC, and Ezekiel 29:17-20 also speaks of God giving Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar. But there is no evidence that Babylon occupied Egypt or destroyed Heliopolis in the way these verses picture, and Egypt remained independent until the Persians conquered it in 525 BC. Interpreters respond in several ways. Some think the Babylonian invasion of about 568 BC did real damage and fulfilled the prophecy in substance, even if the surviving records say little. Others read the prophecy's vivid language (burning temples, wrapping Egypt like a cloak) as the stock imagery of conquest, fulfilled in Babylon's humbling of Egypt rather than in literal detail. Still others hold that some prophecies were fulfilled more fully later, when Persia conquered Egypt. It is fair to say the evidence is incomplete and readers weigh it differently.

questions: The leaders didn't argue with God's message; they simply said it wasn't from God. How do people today dismiss uncomfortable truths by questioning the messenger?
Jeremiah went to Egypt with people who had rejected his word. What does it mean to stay present with people who have made choices you warned them against?
The remnant ran to Egypt looking for safety, but God's word followed them there. Is there anywhere a person can go to escape from God?
